newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan jewellery slump seen pressuring gold imports.
newsitem.headline: Japan jewellery slump seen pressuring gold imports.

text.p: The slump in Japan's jewellery market is likely to keep gold imports at low levels, offsetting a rise in investment buying ahead of an April 1 national sales tax hike, Japanese traders said on Tuesday.
"Gold demand from the investment sector since late February has been rather brisk, partly ahead of the tax hike," said Yukuji Sonoda, president of Sumisho Gold Co Ltd.
"But unsellable inventories at jewellery producers and distributors are being melted down and returned to the bullion market," he said. "This is helping to limit fresh demand for gold."
Japan's gold imports fell 12.3 percent in January from a year earlier to 11.50 tonnes, according to Finance Ministry data, and traders believe imports remained low in February.

Makoto Tonoki, a general manager at Tanaka Kikinzoku Kogyo KK, Japan's largest bullion house, said he estimated Japan's gold imports in February at about nine tonnes, barely half the 17.67 tonnes imported in the same month last year.
The Finance Ministry will release its February import statistics on Friday.
Traders said the slump in Japan's jewellery industry was likely to continue for some time and that more high-profile bankruptcies like those of recent months were looming on the horizon.
This gloomy outlook has made traders particularly reluctant to book imports beyond their immediate needs, market sources said.

"Traders are tending to avoid holding too much inventory due to depressed jewellery demand. With the gold market shrinking, they're also afraid that a large overhang of supplies could depress local bullion premiums, which are currently firm," a trader at a smelting company said. "As a result, they are trying to keep gold imports to a minimum."
Despite low imports, traders said the combination of stock liquidations in the jewellery sector and robust demand and profit-take selling from the investment sector made for brisk local business.

"Gold investment demand has risen, partly due to the upcoming sales tax hike, while private investors who bought gold at lower prices are stepping into the market to take profits," an official at a major bullion house said.
The yen's weaker tendency against the dollar helped push up yen-based retail gold prices in recent months.
The active domestic market was reflected in firm local premiums for gold bullion.

Tokyo spot gold is trading at a premium of about 80 cents an ounce above the London world benchmark price, traders said. Although this represents a retracement from a high of 120 cents in mid-January, it was an improvement over unusually low prices late last year, when Tokyo bullion at times traded at a discount to London.
